elements.quote: “Objectives: We aimed to investigate the psychological problems on people infected with SARS-CoV-2 during the pandemic. Methods: In this living systematic review and meta-analyses,”
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly describes the work as a “living systematic review and meta-analyses.”

elements.quote: “Objectives: We aimed to investigate the psychological problems on people infected with SARS-CoV-2 during the pandemic.”
elements.reason: The abstract provides a clear main objective.
No explicit main inclusion and exclusion criteria are stated in the abstract text provided.
The abstract does not identify information sources (e.g., databases) or report when each source was last searched.

elements.quote: “Methods: In this living systematic review and meta-analyses, we searched seven electronic databases… The primary outcome was prevalence… We pooled data for prevalence with their 95% confidence interval (CI) using random effect models and assessed the study quality based on the 11-item checklist recommended by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality.”
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the risk/study quality assessment approach using an 11-item checklist recommended by AHRQ.

elements.quote: “We pooled data for prevalence with their 95% confidence interval (CI) using random effect models”
elements.reason: The abstract describes methods used to present/synthesize results (random-effects meta-analysis with 95% CIs).

elements.quote: “Results: Fourty-four studies… were identified by comprising a total of 8587 completed questionnaires and 38 studies for meta-analyses.”
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies and participants/questionnaires, and indicates the number included in meta-analyses.

elements.quote: “The prevalence of anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder(PTSD), insomnia, somatization, and fear in patients with COVID-19 was 16.6% (10.1%-23.1%), 37.7% (29.3%-46.2%), 41.5% (9.3%-73.7%), 68.3% (48.6%-88.0%), 36.5% (20.2%-52.8%), 47.6% (9.4%-85.7%), respectively.”
elements.reason: Main outcome results are reported with prevalence estimates and confidence intervals for each outcome.

elements.quote: “we pooled data for prevalence with their 95% confidence interval (CI) using random effect models”
elements.reason: Because meta-analyses were conducted, the abstract reports pooled summary estimates with 95% CIs.

elements.quote: “The prevalence of anxiety, depression, and insomnia in severe COVID-19 patients (intensive care unit inpatients) was higher than mild or clinically stable COVID-19 patients.”
elements.reason: The abstract compares groups, indicating direction of effect and which group has the higher prevalence.

elements.quote: “Limitations: A significant degree of heterogeneity in terms of populations, sampling methods, scales was noted across studies.”
elements.reason: The abstract briefly summarizes an important limitation (heterogeneity across studies).

elements.quote: “Conclusions: There existed high proportions of COVID-19 patients with psychological problem… It is imperative to provide ontime psychological care service for COVID-19 patients and to follow-up them for a longer period.”
elements.reason: The abstract provides interpretation and implications for practice.
No primary source of funding is reported in the provided abstract evidence.
No study register name and registration number are reported in the provided abstract evidence.
No text is provided describing the current state of knowledge and important uncertainties in the context of existing knowledge.
While the abstract states objectives (investigate psychological problems), the retrieved evidence does not explain the importance and need for conducting the review.
The retrieved evidence does not describe whether similar systematic reviews exist and does not explain the need for this review by citing previous reviews/updates.

elements.quote: Objectives: We aimed to investigate the psychological problems on people infected with SARS-CoV-2 during the pandemic.
elements.reason: This is a prevalence/epidemiology review of psychological problems, not a review of intervention effects; therefore the proposed mechanism of action requirement does not apply.

elements.quote: The primary outcome was prevalence of various psychological problems such as anxiety, depression, stress, insomnia, somatization, and fear.
elements.reason: No complex intervention or delivery context is described in the retrieved evidence; thus a logic model of hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes is not applicable.

elements.quote: Objectives: We aimed to investigate the psychological problems on people infected with SARS-CoV-2 during the pandemic.
elements.reason: The review’s objective is explicitly stated in the abstract using a clear objective statement.

The retrieved evidence describes investigation of psychological problems and prevalence using cross-sectional/longitudinal studies, but it does not describe an intervention-effects review or planned comparisons using PICO; therefore this conditional element does not apply based on the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Population: people infected by SARS-CoV-2, regardless of age, gender, race, including suspected SARS-CoV-2 infected patients without a clear nucleic acid diagnosis but with highly suspected clinical performance; Research design: Observational studies, including cross-sectional studies (such as epidemiological survey, questionnaire survey, on­ line survey, etc) and longitudinal studies; Published or pre-print published articles, conference articles or other gray documents; Outcome indicators: prevalence of different psychological problems and associated factors, such as depression, anxiety, stress, insomnia, somatization, and fear.
elements.reason: Eligibility-related study characteristics are specified for population, study design, and outcome indicators; however, relevant components such as eligible settings and follow-up requirements are not explicitly reported in the available evidence.

elements.quote: the COVID-19 mental health database ... included the literature on mental health studies related to COVID-19 since January 1, 2020. The publication language included in the study was English or Chinese.

elements.quote:
To incorporate a study into the meta-analyses, two conditions have to be met: 1) it should determine the results using a recognized scale rather than self-designed question­ naires; 2) the number of result indicators or the scores of specific items in the scale should be accurately reported.

elements.quote: Meta-analyses were performed using Stata v16.0 (StataCorp LLC).

elements.quote: The inverse variance method of DerSimonian and Laird (adjustment) (DerSimonian and Laird, 2015) was adopted to calculate the prevalence rate and the integrated preva­ lence of estimates and 95% confidence interval (CI).

elements.quote: Heterogeneity be­ tween studies was expressed in I 2 ,

elements.quote: We considered using the subgroup analysis for the different stages and degrees of patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection, and divided the patients into overall patients with no dis­ tinguishing feature, patients with mild symptoms or clinically stable patients, severe patients (patients admitted to an intensive care unit diagnosed according to the COVID-19 diagnostic and treatment protocol), discharged patients, patients with suspected infection based on their characteristics; sensitivity analysis was conducted to test the abnormal values that may occur, excluding the research that failed to clearly report the investigation time or survey time point; ... elements.quote: We pooled data for prevalence with their 95% confidence interval (CI) using random effect models... elements.quote: Heterogeneity be­ tween studies was expressed in I 2 , and the results of the meta-analyses were represented by forest plot. elements.quote: The inverse variance method of DerSimonian and Laird (adjustment) (DerSimonian and Laird, 2015) was adopted to calculate the prevalence rate and the integrated preva­ lence of estimates and 95% confidence interval (CI).
elements.reason: The evidence explicitly describes calculated/estimated quantities (prevalence rate and integrated prevalence) using a meta-analytic method, identifying computed results rather than only directly reported values.

elements.quote: The methodology quality scores of all studies included are shown in Table 2. Among these studies, one (2.3%) was rated as high-quality; 33 (75.0%) as medium-quality, and 10 (22.7%) as low-quality.

elements.quote: Results: Fourty-four studies, including studies from China(35), Italy(2), Iran(2), India(1), Korea(1), Ecuador(1), Switzerland(1), Germany(1), were identified by comprising a total of 8587 completed questionnaires and 38 studies for meta-analyses. The prevalence of anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder(PTSD), insomnia, somatization, and fear in patients with COVID-19 was 16.6% (10.1%-23.1%), 37.7% (29.3%-46.2%), 41.5% (9.3%-73.7%), 68.3% (48.6%-88.0%), 36.5% (20.2%-52.8%), 47.6% (9.4%-85.7%), respectively.

elements.quote: However, due to the lack of research into severe patients, the study on psycho­ logical problems of severe patients may have some deficiencies. Although the review has adopted more strict inclusion and exclusion criteria, the original studies included have found significant heteroge­ neity because of the characteristics of observational studies in epidemic situations. The source of heterogeneity was related to the following reasons: the small sample sizes of some studies were small, non-random sampling method, and different survey scales. This research only included one longitudinal study. It was found that the psychological state changes of COVID-19 patients needed long-term follow-up obser­ vation. If possible, more longitudinal studies should be carried out in the future.
elements.reason: The review discusses limitations of the evidence included (e.g., lack of severe-patient research, heterogeneity from observational study characteristics, small samples/non-random sampling/different scales, and only one longitudinal study), but the evidence provided does not clearly show that all limitations are comprehensively covered in the Discussion section specifically.
